strengths: The paper addresses a clear question of interest to researchers studying robust reinforcement learning and epistemic uncertainty. The progression from a constant help action to context-dependent help and sequential driving provides useful, understandable test cases.

The initial experiment supports a meaningful proof of concept: the 1-of-20 policy requests help on 89% of fashion images and 68% of letter images in the single-image regime, while digit accuracy remains 96–99%. Including both single-model and k=N baselines helps distinguish risk aversion from ensembling.

The performance-difference-lemma argument provides a credible basis for extending statewise regret minimization to discounted MDPs with fixed transitions. The manuscript clearly distinguishes epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty and acknowledges its known-transition, tabular-planning, and computational limitations.
weaknesses: Necessary: reconcile contradictory experimental results. For 10% training data and fashion images in the single-image regime, Figure 4 reports approximately 20% help-action frequency for 10-of-10, whereas Figure 21 reports approximately 90% under the same stated conditions. Figure 22 contains similar discrepancies with Figure 4. These differences change the apparent effect of risk aversion and leave the training-data ablation insufficiently supported in the supplied version.

Necessary: correct the probability argument in Appendix B. Equations (11) and (13) have reversed inequality directions, and the positive exponent in (13) produces an impossible negative probability bound. The martingale argument also needs expectations explicitly conditioned on the sampling history. These appear locally repairable, but the high-probability guarantee is not correctly derived as written.

Necessary qualification: Theorems 2 and 4 cover the best or a uniformly sampled iterate, whereas the experiments evaluate the final iterate after 100 iterations. The statement that the policy sequence converges should match the actual guarantee. Plateauing sampled returns provides heuristic support for the experimental stopping rule, but does not establish final-iterate optimality.

Necessary reporting clarification: Appendix A says the all-images 1-of-20 policy requests help for most letters, contradicting the approximately 6% frequency reported in Section 4 and Figure 8. The discussion should also foreground the costs of caution: Table 3 reports 84.13% digit accuracy for 1-of-20 versus 99.28% for 10-of-10 when help is available, and Figure 5 shows that the most robust driving policy nearly stops. These results support a qualified behavioral demonstration, with substantial dependence on evaluation regime and task performance.

Optional improvements: independent ensemble repetitions would better establish reproducibility; the reported ten/five repetitions reshuffle one fitted pool of 2,000 models. Smaller-ensemble ablations would clarify computational requirements, and collision rates per distance traveled would strengthen the practical interpretation of the driving results. These extensions are secondary to resolving the existing reporting contradictions.
